Investors are paying close attention to whether managed-care firms can ease these headaches without losing grip on cost controls. On Tuesday, Reuters said UnitedHealth plans to drop prior approval for 30% of medical services that still require it. UnitedHealthcare plans to roll out the cuts by the end of 2026, targeting select outpatient surgeries, some diagnostic tests—including echocardiograms—and certain outpatient therapies along with chiropractic care. According to the company, just 2% of its medical services now need prior authorization, and roughly 92% of those requests get the green light in under 24 hours on average. UnitedHealthcare CEO Tim Noel called prior authorization “an essential safeguard,” though he added it “should only be used when it truly protects patients and improves care.” The company said it expects over 70% of its prior authorizations to move to a standardized electronic submission process by the end of the year. The shift comes as the broader industry makes a similar push. Back in April, UnitedHealth and CVS Health announced they’d lined up data and submission requirements for over half their prior authorizations. CVS’s Aetna reported 88% of its authorizations were standardized at that point. UnitedHealthcare emphasized that the updates wouldn’t affect coverage criteria or the medical standards for approving or rejecting care. UnitedHealth isn’t dealing with the prior-approval cut in isolation. Just last month, the company posted first-quarter revenue of $111.7 billion, with adjusted earnings landing at $7.23 per share. The full-year adjusted profit outlook climbed above $18.25 a share. Medical cost ratio dropped to 83.9%, down from 84.8% in the same period last year. Analysts saw the report as an early signal of a turnaround for health insurers after a rough patch. Ann Hynes of Mizuho described it as a “positive quarter,” noting that medical cost acceleration seemed to have topped out. Michael Wiederhorn at Oppenheimer, on his end, said UnitedHealth appeared ready to get back to its “beat-and-raise ways.” Reuters Rival headlines set the tone for trading. CVS jumped over 9% after the company boosted its 2026 profit outlook Wednesday, crediting tighter Aetna medical cost controls and a stronger pharmacy-benefit showing. The Aetna medical loss ratio landed at 84.6%, beating analyst forecasts. UnitedHealth and Humana, on the other hand, have both flagged continued pressure from Medicare Advantage costs. There’s risk here. Streamlining approval steps might placate frustrated doctors and patients, but it could open the door to scrutiny over utilization if more services slip past with lighter review. UnitedHealth’s first-quarter materials flagged that both utilization and unit-cost trends stayed high, despite the company touting improved medical cost controls. For UNH stock, it’s not Tuesday’s news that matters most, but how things play out from here. Eyes are on the second-quarter medical cost ratio, the definitive lineup of services dropping prior approval, and whether Medicare Advantage—covering seniors and some disabled Americans—continues the more solid trend seen earlier this year. title: Campus gun carry bill draws out student opinions on both sides - UnionLeader.com
content:
A mix of clouds and sun during the morning will give way to cloudy skies this afternoon. High around 60F. Winds WNW at 10 to 20 mph.. New Hampshire college students turned out both in support and against legislation that would allow students, staff and visitors to legally carry guns and other weapons on any public or private campus that receives government grants. University of New Hampshire Police Chief Steven Lee, inset, speaking at right, testified against legislation to allow anyone to carry weapons on any private or public college that receives government grants. State Rep. Samuel Farrington, R-Rochester, a University of New Hampshire senior, said campus policies restricting guns violate the U.S. Constitution and state law that gives the Legislature the sole authority to restrict access to firearms. “We in New Hampshire have made it crystal clear; self-defense is not a privilege, it is a natural right,” Farrington said Wednesday in presenting his bill (HB 1793). “No government, not a Legislature and certainly not a university bureaucrat, can take away that right.” Beni Griffin, a first-year UNH student, said the campus-carry bill would make the community much more insecure. “This does not increase safety; it increases the likelihood of accidental tragedy,” Griffin said. While Caleb Brower of Mont Vernon, a freshman history student at UNH, said he would have no interest in carrying a gun, he said, “I firmly believe allowing my colleagues to carry weapons on and off campus would further guarantee my own safety.” Both sides cited the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk on a college campus in September to buttress their case. Colin Patterson, a UNH freshman nursing student, said academic buildings are left open during the day, and that leaves students vulnerable. “It is possible that anyone can come in with a gun with bad intention,” said Patterson, who backs the bill. Rep. Timothy Horrigan, D-Durham, pointed out Utah had a similar law in place when Kirk was shot dead while speaking on a college campus. “Utah Valley University was not in fact a gun-free zone, but Kirk’s murderer was able to conceal his rifle on campus and was able to escape without any of the law-abiding citizens being able to return fire,” Horrigan noted. Steven Lee, UNH’s police chief, urged the House Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee to reject the bill and let colleges bar possession of weapons on campuses to maintain order. The campus police force is typically able to respond to an incident within 90 seconds, Lee said. At UNH, students and staff with guns must lock them up at the college police station. They can be taken out for someone to go to a firing range or to use the weapon to legally hunt game, Lee said. “Adding firearms, whether concealed or not, into a devolving dynamic situation is not helpful, not helpful to law enforcement or to the community at large,” Lee said. Dr. John Bunker, a UNH associate dean, said the bill could lead to more suicide incidents, as many students battle mental-health challenges. “College is often a pressure cooker,” Bunker said, adding a short time later, “The greatest threat of gun violence is the risk of self-harm, not an outside shooter.” Michael Glover, a UNH Ph.D. graduate, warned that adopting such a permissive law would prompt many students to leave New Hampshire colleges. “The best and brightest people will not come to this place if you play games like this,” Glover said. Michael Appleton, a Marine veteran and president of the student Senate at the NHTI, said bill opponents brand all students as too immature and weak to be responsible users of firearms. “I am shocked the attitude is that everyone is so suicidally incompetent that they aren’t able to defend their own rights,” Appleton said. What’s Next: The House panel is likely to recommend passage of this bill over the next two months. Outlook: Uncertain. Republican state senators have yet to sign onto the bill and Gov. Kelly Ayotte has yet to weigh in on it.
